article_title: Republicans want to track all student visa holders
article_content:
A Republican lawmaker has proposed legislation that would require colleges and universities to report all non-U.S. citizens enrolled or working at their institutions to the federal government.
Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas has introduced the Educational Visa Transparency Act, which would make universities that receive federal funding submit information on all international students, faculty and administrators to the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS).
SEVIS is a web-based system that the Department of Homeland Security uses to track the immigration status of foreign students while in the U.S., often in the country on F-1 visas.
Reports would be due within 60 days of the bill's enactment and then 30 days after each academic registration period, according to the text of the bill.
"Unmonitored foreign nationals in the labs and research centers of our colleges and universities pose a grave national security threat. My bill will require tracking all student and faculty visas to ensure foreign nationals aren't stealing valuable research," Cotton said in a news release on Tuesday.
The legislation allows officials from the Departments of Education, Justice, Homeland Security and State to access the submitted information for oversight and enforcement. It amends the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act to expand SEVIS reporting requirements for higher education institutions.
The bill has been read twice in the Senate.
State Department Revokes Thousands of Visas
Cracking down on visa-holding students and staff has been a cornerstone of the Trump administration's hard-line approach to immigration. Pro-Palestinian protests at several U.S. college campuses in 2024 and 2025 rocked the nation and led to visa revocations, targeting individuals who expressed support for or attended the demonstrations.
The administration has revoked more than 100,000 visas, including about 8,000 student visas, since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, according to the State Department.
"The State Department has now revoked over 100,000 visas, including some 8,000 student visas and 2,500 specialized visas for individuals who had encounters with U.S. law enforcement for criminal activity. We will continue to deport these thugs to keep America safe," the department wrote on social media on January 12.
The Trump administration has also implemented a suspension of U.S. visas for citizens of 75 countries.
Cases of Alleged Biological Material Smuggling
Foreign nationals on J-1 visas have been charged in recent months with attempting to bring potentially dangerous biological materials into the United States.
Youhuang Xiang, a Chinese researcher, was accused of attempting to bring Escherichia coli (E. coli) into the U.S. without proper authorization, FBI Director Kash Patel said in December.
In November, three Chinese nationals were charged in Michigan after they allegedly tried to smuggle biological materials into the U.S. while conducting research at the University of Michigan. The trio was identified as Xu Bai, Fengfan Zhang and Zhiyong Zhang.
In February, Kseniia Petrova, a Russian-born scientist at Harvard University, was detained after allegedly smuggling frog embryos at Boston Logan International Airport. Her attorney argued that the sample had been brought from Paris and was destined for Harvard, but Petrova had not known she needed to declare it. Petrova was eventually released from custody on the orders of a federal judge.
